parrafos: On Friday, Mom told us that on Saturday we would go to the beach. My brothers and I were happy. We started packing the toys we would take in a bag. My brother Jaime grabbed a beach ball. My little sister Lili packed her favorite doll. I looked for a container to collect snails.
On Saturday we left early. We arrived at a beautiful beach in Loíza.
Mom set our things down under some palm trees. Right away we wanted to take out the toys. Then we realized we had left the bag by the front door. Lili would not stop crying.

After thinking about what we could do without the toys, we decided to build a sandcastle. We used cups to build tall towers. Then we played at swimming like dolphins. Before we knew it, it was time to go back home.

Dogs and cats are two of the most common pets. Both need special care. When taking care of a pet, we must choose a place for it to rest. In that same spot we can put its toys. These are important so the animal can play when it is home alone.
Pets need a feeding routine. The amount of food depends on the size of the animal. If it is big, it will need more food. If it is small, you will need to give it less.
It is important to keep our pets clean. To bathe a dog, you must use special products. You should also use warm water. Cats bathe themselves with just their tongues.
Pets are living beings that become members of the family. It is our duty to take care of them so they can grow up happy and healthy.

segundo-es-03.titulo: The Tadpole and the Little Fish
parrafos: Once upon a time there was a little fish who lived in the Pond of Sighs. One day he met a tadpole. The little fish looked at him in amazement. He saw that the tadpole swam easily thanks to his tail.
The friends spent a lot of time together. They loved to float and let the current carry them. They also liked to hide among the rocks.
One day, the tadpole fell asleep. When he woke up from his long nap, he got a big surprise. He had grown four legs. Soon after, his tail began to shrink until it disappeared.
The tadpole had turned into a frog! Now he could jump everywhere. He still liked to swim, but he also wanted to spend time outside of the pond.
The little fish became very sad. He was afraid of losing his friend. The frog promised that he would visit him every morning.
segundo-es-03.notas: El original dice 'EL sapo' (mayúscula de más) en el último párrafo.

parrafos: Many centuries ago, in the highlands of the Sierra Nevada de Santa Marta, there lived an indigenous tribe known as the Muisca. This tribe was famous for its riches, its knowledge of gold, and its skill at working metal. Among them, a young warrior named Zaque stood out not only for his bravery but also for his wisdom. The story tells that, in a moment of great prosperity, the leader of the Muisca decided to pay tribute to the gods of the sun and the moon, who were revered by the whole community. For this, the Zaque organized a special ceremony in which the tribe's greatest treasure, a large amount of gold, would be given to the gods to ensure the people's prosperity.

On the appointed day, the Zaque entered Lake Guatavita, a sacred lake where, according to tradition, sacrifices to the gods were made. The warrior, dressed in a golden cloak, climbed onto a raft together with his subjects, who carried large amounts of gold. During the ceremony, the Zaque threw the offerings into the water and, as he did so, asked fervently that the tribe continue to prosper in harmony with nature.

The Europeans, who had heard rumors about the fabulous wealth of the Muisca, arrived in the lands of Colombia. With the promise of finding the “golden man,” believing that the Zaque, completely covered in gold, would be the king of a golden kingdom, they began to explore the most remote corners of the mountains, searching tirelessly for the legendary city of El Dorado.

However, the Spaniards never managed to find the lost city. Despite the expeditions and explorations in search of gold, the treasure remained in the waters of the lake, hidden in its depths. The legend of El Dorado went down in history as one of the greatest fables of colonization.

Today, Lake Guatavita is still a place of mystery and fascination. Tourists, eager to find the golden city, come from all over the world, but what they discover is much more than gold: they discover the magic and the history of a people who, although they no longer exist, left a deep mark on the collective imagination.

segundo-es-05.titulo: The Secret of the Jamaican Sea
parrafos: In a small coastal town on the outskirts of Kingston, Jamaica, lived a young girl named María, known for her contagious joy and her endless curiosity. She had always felt a special connection to the sea. Since she was little, her grandmother had told her stories about the ocean and its mysteries. She said that the Jamaican sea was not only beautiful but also hid secrets that only people with a pure heart could discover.

One afternoon, while walking along the beach after school, María saw an old fisherman sitting near his boat. His name was Uncle Bennie, a man who was wise and respected by everyone in the town. She had always heard rumors about him: it was said that he knew the deepest secrets of the sea and that he had spent his life searching for something valuable that he had never shared.
María approached with a smile and asked him:
“Uncle Bennie, what is it that the sea keeps that everyone says is so important?”
The old man looked at her with eyes full of untold stories. After a long silence, he smiled and said:
“The sea has a treasure, child, but it is not gold or jewels. The true treasure lies in its secrets, in the magic it offers only to those who are willing to listen.”
Intrigued, María decided she had to find out what that mystery was.

That night, when the moon was full and the waves whispered softly, she ventured out alone into the sea. She told no one, not even her grandmother, because she knew she had to do it for herself. Her grandmother always told her: “The sea does not give up its secrets easily. You have to earn them with your heart and soul.”

María swam to where the waves seemed calmest. Suddenly, she saw something strange: a bright blue light glowing under the water. The girl swam toward it, following the light that moved with the rhythm of the waves. As she got closer, the light grew stronger, and María felt a strange calm run through her body.

Finally, she reached a small coral reef, where the light seemed to come from. As she got closer, she saw an enormous shell, much bigger than any other she had seen on the beach. Very carefully, she took it in her hands. Suddenly, the light shone intensely, and María heard a soft voice whispering:

“You have found the heart of the sea. Its secret is simple, child: the beauty of Jamaica, its people, its culture, its music… everything is connected to nature. The sea only shows you its treasure if you learn to listen to what surrounds you.”

María, amazed, looked around. At that moment, the sea seemed to speak to her in its own language. She could hear the whisper of the waves, the singing of the birds, and the vibration of the drums in the distance. It was a harmonious sound, like a song coming from the earth itself.

That night, as she returned to the shore, María understood the message of the sea. The true treasure was not in material things but in the deep connection with her people, her culture, and the land around them.
From then on, she shared her discovery with others, and the town, inspired by María's revelation, began to celebrate life, nature, and the spirit of Jamaica with more joy and gratitude than ever.

And so, the secret of the Jamaican sea kept living on in the songs of the drums, in the laughter of children running along the beach, and in the stories told at sunset, where every wave seemed to bring a message of hope and unity.
segundo-es-05.notas: 'Tio Bennie' (sin tilde en el original) se tradujo como 'Uncle Bennie'.

parrafos: The coquí, a small frog endemic to Puerto Rico, does not have an institutional origin as a symbol, but it is deeply representative of Puerto Rican culture. This animal, whose song is characteristic of the island, is an unofficial but widely recognized symbol of Puerto Rican identity. Its name comes from the sound it makes, “co-quí,” and its song has become a cultural icon that evokes the vibrant and unique nature of Puerto Rico. Although it is not an official symbol, the coquí is widely used in Puerto Rican literature, music, and art.

The maga tree was proclaimed the national tree of Puerto Rico in 1956. This tree, whose scientific name is Thespesia grandiflora, is native to the island and has bright purple flowers that are greatly admired for their beauty. The maga symbolizes the island's native flora and natural wealth. Its symbolism is linked to the identity and love of nature of Puerto Ricans, and it is a common figure in the literature and cultural representations of the island.

Known since colonial times as the “Key to the Gulf” because of its closeness to the entrance of the Gulf of Mexico, Cuba is the largest island of the Greater Antilles and is part of the archipelago known as the Republic of Cuba. Alongside it, another of the most notable islands is the Isle of Youth, as well as many different keys such as Cayo Coco, Cayo Largo del Sur, or Cayo Guillermo. With a seasonally humid tropical climate and a notable maritime influence, it is located at a latitude very close to the Tropic of Cancer, which determines the high levels of solar radiation it receives and the warm character of its climate. Its capital, Havana, is the heart of the festivities, a city to be lived at night and strolled through by day. You cannot miss the Malecón, the Old Cathedral, the mojitos at La Bodeguita del Medio, the Vedado neighborhood, the Morro Castle park, and the delicious ice cream at Coppelia. Another must-see is Varadero, one of the most famous coastal areas of this island, with keys such as Cayo Guillermo, Cayo Coco, or Cayo Largo being especially important.

The name of the island of Cuba comes from the term “Cubao,” which means “where the land is abundant.” In this place there are more than 14,000 different species of animals, and the smallest amphibian in the world, known as the pygmy frog or little toad, lives here, measuring less than 12 mm in length.

Cuba was discovered by Christopher Columbus in 1492 and, like other Caribbean islands, was colonized by the Spanish. Cuba became independent from Spain in 1898 after the Spanish-American War, but later became a communist state in 1959 with the Cuban Revolution led by Fidel Castro. Cuba's economy has historically depended on agriculture, particularly sugar cane and tobacco, although in recent decades tourism and economic reforms have become more important. The island is also famous for its rum production and its pharmaceutical industry.

Cuba is known for its music, such as son, salsa, mambo, and rumba, and for its dance and literary traditions. Che (Ernesto Guevara), one of the main icons of the Cuban Revolution, and Cuban dance and music are symbols of its rich cultural heritage.
segundo-es-08.notas: Texto informativo con algunas imprecisiones en el original (p. ej. 'archipiélago conocido como República de Cuba', 'Isla Juventud'); se tradujo fielmente. 'Cubao' y los nombres de lugares se dejaron como en el original.

segundo-es-09.titulo: Fable: The Tortoise and the Rabbit of the Panama Canal
parrafos: On the green plains near the Panama Canal, a very fast rabbit and a very wise tortoise lived together, although their ways of life were very different.
One day, while they were walking near the waters of the canal, the rabbit, full of pride in his speed, boasted:
“I am the fastest animal in all of Panama! No one can beat me in a race!”
The tortoise, known for her slowness but also for her cleverness, decided it was time to teach the vain rabbit a lesson.
“If you are so fast, why don't we have a race?” the tortoise proposed.
The rabbit, laughing at the idea that a tortoise could compete with him, accepted the challenge without thinking twice.
“I'm going to beat you easily!” said the rabbit, sure of his victory.
The starting line was drawn near the canal, among the trees of the tropical forests. All the animals of the forest, including some birds and curious monkeys, gathered to watch the competition.

The race began, and as expected, the rabbit quickly took the lead. He ran so fast that he soon disappeared from the tortoise's sight. However, the rabbit, confident that his lead was unbeatable, decided to rest a little in the shade of a tree, near a beautiful river that flowed through the forest.

The tortoise, at her slow but steady pace, kept going without stopping. As she advanced, she took in the scenery, the colors of the birds, and the beautiful trees that decorated the Panamanian forest.
Meanwhile, the rabbit kept sleeping.

When he finally woke up, he saw that the tortoise had almost reached the finish line. Desperate, he began to run at full speed, but it was too late. The tortoise had already crossed the finish line and won the race.
The animals that had watched the race celebrated the tortoise's victory, and she smiled and said:
“Patience and perseverance always beat haste and arrogance.”

Once upon a time, in a small Mexican town, there was a boy named Pedro. Pedro lived in a modest house with his mom and dad, who worked hard to give him what he needed to live. Although his parents were not rich, they always made sure that Pedro had food, clean clothes, and a school to attend.

Pedro was a dreamer. Every day after school, he sat in front of his house to watch the children of the town playing with their new toys. There was a boy named Luis who had a shiny red bicycle. Pedro could not stop looking at it with envy. He thought that if he had that bicycle, his life would be much better.

One day, while Pedro was walking through the market with his mom, he saw a cart full of toys. There, a soccer ball shone, so big and colorful that he could hardly stop looking at it. “Mom, please, buy me that ball! It will be the best gift of all!” Pedro exclaimed.
His mom, with a warm smile, stroked his head and said to him:

“Pedro, that ball is a lovely wish, but remember that at home we have an old soccer ball we can use to play, and we have enough to eat and to study. That is the most important thing so that you can have a better future.”

Pedro felt a little sad, but he understood. They went back home and Pedro saw the old ball his mom had mentioned. Although it was a bit worn, it was perfect for playing. That afternoon, Pedro and his mom went to the park and started playing with the ball. Pedro realized that, even though he did not have the new ball, he was having a lot of fun and was grateful for what he had.
A few days later, when Pedro saw Luis with his red bicycle again, he asked him: “Luis, do you like your bicycle a lot?”
Luis smiled and answered: “Of course! But what I like most is being able to play with my friends. The bicycle is fun, but it is not the only thing that makes me happy.”

Pedro, hearing those words, understood that sometimes wishes, although exciting, are not the most important thing. The needs of his life, like having a family who loved him, an education, and a roof over his head, were what truly made him happy.

In time, Pedro learned to value what he had, and although he kept dreaming of many things, he understood that what was essential was what made him feel safe and loved. In this way, he learned to tell the difference between what he truly needed to be happy and what he only wanted for moments.
In the bay, proud and serene,
a flame rises that never grieves.
With open arms and a gaze toward the sea,
she seems to keep eternal hope.
Her torch lights the path to follow,
a promise of a world yet to build.
Forged from copper and from dreams,
the Statue of Liberty, forever admired.
segundo-es-11.notas: Poema: traducción literal, no conserva la rima.

parrafos: Under the blue sky of endless vastness,
your landscapes stretch out, blessed land.
From the rocky mountains to the roaring sea,
you are a cradle of dreams, a shared world.
Your golden prairies, vast and serene,
whisper stories of those who break chains.
Your rivers sing of freedom with mighty force,
and the wind carries a brave spirit.
You are a mosaic of voices, of races and colors,
of languages that intertwine a thousand flavors.
New York and its glow, a beacon of ambition,
Hollywood and its stars, a cradle of illusion.
United States, vast and diverse place,
on your wings of freedom we want to fly.
With lights and shadows, promises and dreams,
you remain a world of eternal paths.
segundo-es-12.notas: Poema: traducción literal, no conserva la rima.

parrafos: Clara left school just as it started to rain.
She opened her red umbrella and walked toward the bus stop.
There she found Bruno, who was waiting under a small roof.
“Do you want to walk with me?” Clara asked.
Bruno accepted, but the umbrella barely covered the two of them.
So they walked more slowly and stayed close so they would not get wet.
When they reached the corner, they saw a woman looking for shelter.
Clara and Bruno walked her to a nearby store.
When the rain stopped, the three of them smiled.
Clara understood that sharing does not always mean having a lot; sometimes it is enough to make room for someone else.
Diego and Gabriela were walking near a stream when they discovered a seed among the rocks.
They decided to take it to the school garden.
First they asked their teacher how to plant it.
Then they prepared the soil and watered it without wasting water.
Several days went by with no change.
Diego thought the seed would not grow, but Gabriela asked for patience.
A week later, a green sprout appeared.
The children put up a sign so that no one would step on it.
In time, the plant grew its first leaves.
Diego understood that protecting nature takes information, perseverance, and care.
